Both offer native expiry: Redis EXPIRE/SET EX, and DynamoDB TTL on an epoch-seconds attribute. Their timing guarantees differ a lot (see L-0070).

Right for Redis, misleading for DynamoDB. DynamoDB TTL is a lazy background process: AWS says expired items are deleted 'typically within a few days', and until then they still come back from reads, so 'absent = offline' does not hold. With DynamoDB you must store an epoch-seconds expiry attribute on every heartbeat and treat expiry < now as offline at read time (filter expressions for Query/Scan). With Redis, a plain SET clears the existing TTL; write SET key v EX 30 (or SET then EXPIRE) on every heartbeat. Redis expiry is accurate to within about 1 ms.
precise_version: Redis: SET user:<id> 1 EX 30 on each heartbeat, so the key vanishes 30 s after the last one. DynamoDB: store expires_at = now+30 and treat expires_at < now as offline, because TTL deletion can lag by days.

6M updates/minute is 100k writes/s. Whether that 'chokes' depends on the store: a single Redis instance does roughly 70k-180k SET/s in the official benchmark without pipelining, and over 1.5M/s with pipelining. A disk-based relational database committing 100k durable single-row updates per second is much harder. The concern is real for an RDBMS and less so for an in-memory key-value store.

precise_version: The whole dataset is tiny (8 MB for 1 million active entries, 8 GB even for 1 billion users), while 6 million writes per minute is the real challenge.

Counts are off. Opening is the three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK: 1 round trip before the client can send). Closing is FIN and ACK from each side: normally four segments, three when a FIN and ACK are combined (RFC 9293 3.6). So the total is about 6-7 segments, not 5. What matters for latency is the extra round trips before the first query: the TCP handshake plus the database's authentication exchange, and TLS when used.
precise_version: A fresh connection costs a TCP handshake (one round trip), the database login exchange (and TLS if used) and a FIN/ACK teardown. Pooling skips all of that on every request.

The kernel's TCP stack handles the SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK packets, not the database process. The expensive part for the database is what follows: PostgreSQL spawns a backend process per connection, MySQL allocates a thread with its own stack and connection/result buffers, and both run authentication. Those are the CPU and memory costs pooling avoids.
precise_version: Opening a connection costs the database a new backend process or thread, buffers and an authentication exchange, on top of the kernel's TCP handshake.

note: Memory is part of the cost too. Each MySQL connection thread gets its own stack plus connection and result buffers, and each PostgreSQL connection is a separate process. AWS RDS states 'database connections consume memory' and derives the default max_connections from instance memory. AWS also describes pooling as avoiding 'the memory and CPU overhead' of new connections. The teacher's 'not really memory' self-correction goes too far.

HikariCP calls this idleTimeout; its default is exactly 10 minutes, and it applies only when minimumIdle is below maximumPoolSize. A separate maxLifetime (default 30 min) retires even busy connections.

An in-process library is the common case, but external poolers exist and run as separate services: PgBouncer ('lightweight connection pooler for PostgreSQL') and Amazon RDS Proxy. They are the usual fix for the problem in L-0319/L-0320: many app servers multiplexed onto a few database connections.

The pushback against 'everything is a service' is fair for the in-app library pool, but pooling is sometimes deliberately run as a separate service (PgBouncer, Amazon RDS Proxy), when many servers or serverless functions would otherwise exhaust the database's connections.

Query time is key (pool size needed is roughly throughput x average query time), but also track pool wait time and saturation. HikariCP's sizing guide ties the optimum to database cores and disks: past it, adding connections lowers throughput.

Student proposal, left open. Often the wrong move: if average query time rises because the database is saturated, a bigger pool adds concurrent load and makes it worse. precise_version: If query time rises, first find out why; enlarging the pool helps only when the database has spare capacity and requests are queuing for connections.
